docs.title: FrostWatch
docs.text:
Free, open source Snowflake cost optimization and observability. Self-hosted.

Find your Snowflake savings in 60 seconds

pip install frostwatch
frostwatch audit --connection <your_snowflake_connection>
Read-only, no server, no LLM key. You get a ranked list of savings with dollar estimates and the SQL to fix each one. See a sample report · No-install SQL version · How it works

Then keep it fixed. FrostWatch connects to your Snowflake account, pulls from SNOWFLAKE.ACCOUNT_USAGE, and gives you a dark-themed web dashboard with:

  • 💰 Savings Advisor: rule-based checks across warehouses, storage and cloud services with $ estimates and fix SQL
  • 📊 Cost breakdown by warehouse, user, and query tag
  • 🚨 Anomaly detection — spend spikes vs. a 21-day rolling baseline per warehouse
  • 🤖 AI explanations — plain-English summaries for each anomaly (BYO LLM: Claude, GPT-4o, Gemini, or local Ollama)
  • 🔍 Query fingerprinting — group near-identical queries by SQL pattern and surface the patterns driving the most spend
  • 📉 Week-over-week regression detection — flag query patterns that became more expensive this week vs last (medium / high / critical)
  • 📈 Cost forecasting — per-warehouse credit projections using linear regression on historical data
  • ✏️ AI query rewrites — LLM-powered optimized SQL, root-cause analysis, and estimated savings for any expensive query
  • 📦 dbt model costs — per-model credit and performance breakdown parsed from query_tag
  • 📬 Weekly digest delivered to Slack or email
  • 🔌 REST API for integration with your own tooling

docs.title: Quick start
docs.text:
pipDockerdocker compose 
pip install frostwatch
frostwatch config init    # creates ~/.frostwatch/config.yaml
frostwatch serve          # starts on http://localhost:8000

docker run -p 8000:8000 \
  -e FROSTWATCH_SNOWFLAKE_ACCOUNT=xy12345.us-east-1 \
  -e FROSTWATCH_SNOWFLAKE_USER=myuser \
  -e FROSTWATCH_SNOWFLAKE_PASSWORD=mypass \
  -e FROSTWATCH_LLM_API_KEY=sk-ant-... \
  ghcr.io/arunrajiah/frostwatch

curl -O https://raw.githubusercontent.com/arunrajiah/frostwatch/main/docker-compose.yml
# Edit docker-compose.yml to set your env vars
docker compose up

Then open http://localhost:8000.

docs.title: POST /api/insights/rewrites
docs.text:
Submits an expensive query to your configured LLM and returns an optimization report. Results are persisted and returned idempotently — calling this endpoint twice for the same query_id returns the cached result without making a second LLM call.

Request body:

{ "query_id": "01b2c3d4-..." }

Response — QueryRewriteResponse:

{
  "id": 1,
  "query_id": "01b2c3d4-...",
  "fingerprint": "a3f1b2c4...",
  "rewrite_suggestion": "## Rewrite
```sql
SELECT id, status, ...```

## Root Cause
...

## Recommendations
- Add clustering key on STATUS
...

## Estimated Savings
40–60% credit reduction",
  "generated_at": "2026-05-04T10:00:00Z"
}

Returns 503 if no LLM provider is configured, 404 if the query_id is not found, 404 if no rewrite exists yet (use POST to generate one).

docs.title: Chaos Genius alternative
docs.text:
Looking for a maintained, open source replacement for Chaos Genius to watch your Snowflake spend? FrostWatch is MIT licensed, self-hosted, and actively developed.

The open source Chaos Genius repository was archived in September 2024 and is no longer maintained. If you used it to keep an eye on Snowflake costs, or you are looking for an open source option after evaluating Chaos Genius's commercial Snowflake product, this page explains what carries over and how to switch.

docs.title: Is FrostWatch the right replacement?
docs.text:
Chaos Genius was a general-purpose anomaly detection and root cause engine: you pointed it at any data source and defined the KPIs and dimensions yourself. FrostWatch is Snowflake-specific: it reads SNOWFLAKE.ACCOUNT_USAGE directly, so cost metrics, dimensions, and baselines work with no modeling on your side.

  • Switch to FrostWatch if the main thing you monitored was Snowflake spend, warehouse usage, or query cost.
  • Look elsewhere if you monitored business KPIs (daily active users, revenue, failure rates) or data outside Snowflake. FrostWatch does not cover those.

docs.title: Feature mapping
docs.text:
What you used in Chaos Genius FrostWatch equivalent Anomaly detection on a cost KPI Per-warehouse spend anomaly detection against a rolling 21-day baseline, with severity levels Multidimensional drill-downs Cost by warehouse, user, role, query tag, and dbt model Automated root cause analysis Plain-English LLM explanations for each anomaly, query fingerprinting to find the SQL patterns driving spend, and week-over-week regression detection Smart alerting Weekly digests to Slack or email, dbt model spend thresholds, and resource monitor limit warnings Forecasting (was on the Chaos Genius roadmap) Per-warehouse credit forecasts for the next 1 to 30 days Self-hosted with Docker Self-hosted with Docker or pip install; data stays in your infrastructure

FrostWatch also adds Snowflake-specific tools Chaos Genius did not have:

  • dbt model cost attribution, dbt Cloud job and environment breakdowns, and a cost summary posted on pull requests
  • AI query rewrites with optimized SQL and estimated savings
  • Resource monitor recommendations with ready-to-run CREATE RESOURCE MONITOR DDL
  • Per-user and per-role budgets
  • Bring your own LLM: Anthropic, OpenAI, Gemini, or a fully local Ollama model

docs.title: Migrating
docs.text:
There is no data to export. FrostWatch reads history straight from Snowflake's ACCOUNT_USAGE views, which keep up to a year of query and metering history, so your first sync already has a baseline.

1. Try it with synthetic data first (no Snowflake needed):

pip install frostwatch
frostwatch demo
# open http://localhost:8000

2. Create a read-only role. FrostWatch never writes to Snowflake:

CREATE ROLE frostwatch_role;
GRANT IMPORTED PRIVILEGES ON DATABASE SNOWFLAKE TO ROLE frostwatch_role;
GRANT ROLE frostwatch_role TO USER your_user;

3. Configure and start:

frostwatch config init    # creates ~/.frostwatch/config.yaml
frostwatch serve          # starts on http://localhost:8000

Add your Snowflake credentials, an LLM key (or an Ollama URL), and your Slack webhook or SMTP settings to the config. See Configuration for every option, or Installation for Docker.

docs.title: Questions
docs.text: Open an issue. If something you relied on in Chaos Genius is missing, tell us: it helps decide what goes on the roadmap.

docs.title: Configuration
docs.text: FrostWatch is configured via ~/.frostwatch/config.yaml. Every field can also be set via an environment variable prefixed FROSTWATCH_ — environment variables take precedence over the YAML file.

docs.title: Full reference
docs.text:
# ── Snowflake connection ──────────────────────────────────────────────────────
snowflake_account: "xy12345.us-east-1"     # Your Snowflake account identifier
snowflake_user: "your_username"
snowflake_password: "your_password"        # Or FROSTWATCH_SNOWFLAKE_PASSWORD
snowflake_warehouse: "COMPUTE_WH"
snowflake_database: "SNOWFLAKE"            # Built-in SNOWFLAKE database
snowflake_schema: "ACCOUNT_USAGE"          # Leave as-is
snowflake_role: "ACCOUNTADMIN"             # Needs SELECT on ACCOUNT_USAGE

# ── LLM configuration ────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
# Supported providers: anthropic | openai | gemini | ollama
llm_provider: "anthropic"
llm_model: ""                              # Leave empty to use provider default
llm_api_key: "sk-ant-..."                  # Or FROSTWATCH_LLM_API_KEY
llm_base_url: "http://localhost:11434"     # Only used for ollama provider

# ── Alerts ────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
slack_webhook_url: ""                      # https://hooks.slack.com/services/...
email_smtp_host: ""                        # e.g. smtp.gmail.com
email_smtp_port: 587
email_smtp_user: ""
email_smtp_password: ""
email_recipients:
  - "data-team@yourcompany.com"

# ── Scheduling ────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
schedule_cron: "0 8 * * 1"    # Weekly digest (default: Monday 8am)
sync_cron: "0 */6 * * *"      # Data sync (default: every 6 hours)
snowflake_query_limit: 500    # Max queries fetched per sync

# ── Anomaly detection ─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
alert_threshold_multiplier: 3.0  # Flag spend > 3× rolling baseline

# ── Cost ──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
credits_per_dollar: 3.0           # USD per credit (legacy name). Adjust for your contract rate

# ── Server ────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
cors_origins:
  - "http://localhost:5173"
  - "http://127.0.0.1:5173"
  # Add your deployment URL for production:
  # - "https://frostwatch.yourcompany.com"

# ── Storage ───────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
data_dir: "~/.frostwatch"         # SQLite database and logs location

docs.title: LLM providers
docs.text:
Provider llm_provider Default model Notes Anthropic anthropic claude-sonnet-4-6 Recommended OpenAI openai gpt-4o Google Gemini gemini gemini-2.0-flash Ollama (local) ollama llama3 Set llm_base_url to your Ollama endpoint

LLM is used for anomaly explanations and AI query rewrites (POST /api/insights/rewrites). FrostWatch functions without it — anomalies are still detected and all other insights (fingerprinting, regressions, forecasts) still work, just without LLM-generated summaries or rewrite suggestions.

docs.title: Environment variables
docs.text:
All config fields are available as env vars by uppercasing the field name and adding the FROSTWATCH_ prefix:

export FROSTWATCH_SNOWFLAKE_ACCOUNT=xy12345.us-east-1
export FROSTWATCH_SNOWFLAKE_PASSWORD=secret
export FROSTWATCH_LLM_API_KEY=sk-ant-...

This is the recommended approach for Docker and Kubernetes deployments.

docs.title: Production deployment
docs.text:
For production add your deployment URL to cors_origins:

cors_origins:
  - "https://frostwatch.yourcompany.com"

Or via env var (comma-separated):

FROSTWATCH_CORS_ORIGINS=https://frostwatch.yourcompany.com

docs.title: Snowflake authentication
docs.text:
Password-only logins are being phased out by Snowflake (MFA enforcement). Use one of:

# Reuse a named connection from ~/.snowflake/connections.toml (same file the Snowflake CLI uses)
snowflake_connection_name: my_conn

# SSO through your identity provider (opens a browser once; token is cached)
snowflake_authenticator: externalbrowser

# Key-pair auth, recommended for servers and service users
snowflake_private_key_path: /secrets/rsa_key.p8
snowflake_private_key_passphrase: ""   # or FROSTWATCH_SNOWFLAKE_PRIVATE_KEY_PASSPHRASE

Precedence: connection name, then private key, then authenticator, then password.

docs.title: dbt Cloud Integration
docs.text: Connect FrostWatch to the dbt Cloud API to get run-level cost attribution, per-job and per-environment breakdowns, model spend threshold alerts, and manifest-enriched model metadata.

docs.title: Configuration
docs.text:
# ~/.frostwatch/config.yaml
dbt_cloud_account_id: "12345"          # Your dbt Cloud account ID (Settings → Account)
dbt_cloud_api_token: "dbtc_..."        # Service token with Viewer access
dbt_model_credit_threshold: 0.5        # Alert when a model exceeds this many credits/day (0 = disabled)

Or via environment variables:

export FROSTWATCH_DBT_CLOUD_ACCOUNT_ID=12345
export FROSTWATCH_DBT_CLOUD_API_TOKEN=dbtc_...
export FROSTWATCH_DBT_MODEL_CREDIT_THRESHOLD=0.5

docs.title: Syncing run metadata
docs.text:
curl -X POST http://localhost:8000/api/dbt/sync-cloud

Returns {"runs_synced": N, "jobs_enriched": N, "environments_enriched": N}.

FrostWatch pulls the last 30 days of runs and attributes Snowflake credits to each run by summing dbt-tagged queries whose start_time falls inside the run window.

docs.title: Cost breakdown by job and environment
docs.text:
Endpoint What it shows GET /api/dbt/jobs Credits, cost, run count, avg duration, last-run status per job GET /api/dbt/environments Credits, cost, run count, distinct jobs per environment GET /api/dbt/runs Individual runs with full metadata, newest first

All three endpoints accept a ?days= parameter (1–90, default 30).

docs.title: Spend threshold alerts
docs.text:
Set dbt_model_credit_threshold in your config to a positive value. After every Snowflake sync, FrostWatch checks each dbt model's total credits for the current calendar day. If any model exceeds the threshold, an alert is created.

GET /api/dbt/threshold-alerts

Example response:

[
  {
    "id": 1,
    "detected_at": "2026-05-04T23:59:00Z",
    "dbt_model": "revenue_daily",
    "period_start": "2026-05-04T00:00:00Z",
    "period_end": "2026-05-04T23:59:00Z",
    "credits_used": 0.612,
    "threshold": 0.3
  }
]

docs.title: Manifest enrichment
docs.text:
Upload your manifest.json to add owner, description, materialization type, and tags to every model in FrostWatch.

curl -X POST http://localhost:8000/api/dbt/manifest \
     -H "Content-Type: application/json" \
     --data-binary @target/manifest.json

Automate this in CI (add after dbt run or dbt compile):

- name: Upload dbt manifest to FrostWatch
  run: |
    curl -X POST "${{ secrets.FROSTWATCH_URL }}/api/dbt/manifest" \
         -H "Content-Type: application/json" \
         --data-binary @target/manifest.json

Retrieve enriched metadata:

GET /api/dbt/metadata

docs.title: PR cost comment (GitHub Actions)
docs.text:
The bundled workflow .github/workflows/dbt-cost-comment.yml posts a dbt model cost table + threshold alerts as a PR comment after every dbt run.

Setup:

  1. Add a FROSTWATCH_URL repository secret.
  2. In the workflow file, update workflow_run.workflows to match the name of your dbt workflow.
  3. Ensure FrostWatch is reachable from your CI runner.

The comment is edited on subsequent runs — one comment per PR, always up to date.

docs.title: Required GitHub Actions permissions
docs.text:
permissions:
  pull-requests: write

docs.title: Third-party actions used
docs.text:
• peter-evans/find-comment@v3
  • peter-evans/create-or-update-comment@v4

docs.title: dbt Integration
docs.text:
FrostWatch provides two layers of dbt integration:

  1. Automatic model attribution — parse the query_tag Snowflake sets on every dbt query and group credits by model name. Zero config required.
  2. dbt Cloud deep-dive — connect to the dbt Cloud API to get run-level metadata, cost breakdown by job and environment, spend threshold alerts, and manifest-enriched model metadata.

docs.title: Automatic model attribution
docs.text:
When dbt runs a model against Snowflake, it sets the QUERY_TAG session parameter to a JSON string such as:

{
  "app": "dbt",
  "dbt_version": "1.8.0",
  "profile_name": "my_project",
  "target_name": "prod",
  "node_id": "model.my_project.orders"
}

FrostWatch parses this tag during each sync and extracts the model name from node_id. Both the flat format above and the nested dbt_snowflake_query_tags wrapper are supported.

dbt sets query_tag automatically for Snowflake connections from dbt-snowflake v1.0 onwards — no extra configuration needed.

docs.title: The dbt Models page
docs.text:
Once FrostWatch has synced data containing dbt query tags, the dbt Models page shows:

  • Models detected — total number of distinct dbt models observed
  • Total credits — Snowflake credits consumed across all dbt models
  • Bar chart — top 15 models by credit consumption
  • Detail table — credits, USD cost, query count, and average execution time per model

docs.title: Backfilling existing data
docs.text:
frostwatch sync
# or click Sync Now in the sidebar

The sync upsert updates dbt_model on every re-synced query, so existing rows are enriched automatically.

docs.title: Supported node types
docs.text: Only model nodes are tracked. Seeds (seed.*), snapshots (snapshot.*), tests (test.*), and other node types are ignored.

docs.title: Setup
docs.text:
Add the following to your ~/.frostwatch/config.yaml:

dbt_cloud_account_id: "12345"           # Your dbt Cloud account ID
dbt_cloud_api_token: "dbtc_..."         # Service token with read access
dbt_model_credit_threshold: 0.5        # Alert when a model exceeds 0.5 credits/day (0 = disabled)

Or via environment variables:

export FROSTWATCH_DBT_CLOUD_ACCOUNT_ID=12345
export FROSTWATCH_DBT_CLOUD_API_TOKEN=dbtc_...
export FROSTWATCH_DBT_MODEL_CREDIT_THRESHOLD=0.5

docs.title: Syncing dbt Cloud metadata
docs.text:
Trigger a one-off sync from the dbt Cloud API:

curl -X POST http://localhost:8000/api/dbt/sync-cloud

This pulls the last 30 days of runs, enriches them with job and environment names, and attributes Snowflake credits to each run by matching dbt-tagged queries inside the run time window.

docs.title: Cost breakdown by job and environment
docs.text:
GET /api/dbt/jobs — credits, cost, run count, avg duration, and last-run status per job.

GET /api/dbt/environments — credits, cost, run count, and distinct job count per environment.

docs.title: Spend threshold alerts
docs.text:
When dbt_model_credit_threshold is set (> 0), FrostWatch checks at the end of every Snowflake sync whether any dbt model exceeded its daily credit limit. Violations are stored and returned by GET /api/dbt/threshold-alerts.

Set a per-model threshold in your config:

dbt_model_credit_threshold: 0.5   # flag any model that uses > 0.5 credits today

docs.title: Manifest enrichment
docs.text:
Upload your manifest.json to enrich the dbt model catalogue with owner, description, materialization type, and tags — metadata that isn't available in Snowflake's QUERY_HISTORY.

curl -X POST http://localhost:8000/api/dbt/manifest \
     -H "Content-Type: application/json" \
     --data-binary @target/manifest.json

Returns {"models_upserted": N}. The enriched catalogue is available at GET /api/dbt/metadata.

You can automate this in your dbt CI pipeline:

# In your dbt GitHub Actions workflow, after dbt compile or dbt run:
- name: Upload manifest to FrostWatch
  run: |
    curl -X POST "${{ secrets.FROSTWATCH_URL }}/api/dbt/manifest" \
         -H "Content-Type: application/json" \
         --data-binary @target/manifest.json

docs.title: GitHub Actions — PR cost comments
docs.text:
The bundled workflow .github/workflows/dbt-cost-comment.yml posts a dbt model cost summary and threshold alert table as a PR comment after every dbt run.

Setup:

  1. Add a FROSTWATCH_URL repository secret pointing to your FrostWatch instance.
  2. Edit the workflow_run.workflows trigger to match the name of your dbt workflow.
  3. Ensure your FrostWatch instance is reachable from GitHub Actions (or use a self-hosted runner on the same network).

The comment is edited (not duplicated) on subsequent runs using peter-evans/create-or-update-comment.

docs.title: Query Insights
docs.text: The Insights feature set (introduced in v0.2.0) gives you a deeper understanding of which query patterns are driving Snowflake spend, how that spend has changed, and what to do about it — all without writing SQL yourself.

docs.title: Query fingerprinting
docs.text:
FrostWatch normalizes every query in your history to a canonical form:

  1. Strip -- and /* */ comments
  2. Replace string literals with '?'
  3. Collapse IN (...) value lists to IN (?)
  4. Replace numeric literals with ?
  5. Collapse whitespace and uppercase

The result is an MD5 fingerprint that groups queries that differ only in bind values or formatting into a single pattern. For example, these three queries all map to the same fingerprint:

SELECT * FROM orders WHERE id = 123
SELECT * FROM orders WHERE id = 456
SELECT * FROM orders WHERE id = 789

The Insights → Fingerprints page shows the top patterns by total credits, with per-pattern stats: total and average credits, execution count, first/last seen, and the most frequent warehouse and user.

API endpoint: GET /api/insights/fingerprints?days=30&limit=20

docs.title: Week-over-week regression detection
docs.text:
FrostWatch compares the average credits per execution for each fingerprint between the current week and the previous week. Patterns that grew beyond a configurable threshold are flagged with a severity label:

Ratio (this week / last week) Severity 2× – 2.9× medium 3× – 4.9× high ≥ 5× critical

This catches situations where a query hasn't changed in code but is suddenly scanning much more data — a sign of missing filters, table bloat, or clustering drift.

API endpoint: GET /api/insights/regressions?threshold=2.0&limit=10

docs.title: Cost forecasting
docs.text:
FrostWatch fits an ordinary least-squares regression to each warehouse's daily credit history and projects forward. Each forecast point includes:

  • Predicted credits and USD cost for each future day
  • Trend — up, down, or stable (based on the regression slope)
  • Confidence — low (fewer than 7 data points), medium (7–13), or high (14+)
  • Projected 30-day totals — helpful for budget planning

Forecasts use the credits_per_dollar value from your config (default: 3.0).

API endpoint: GET /api/insights/forecasts?days_ahead=7&history_days=30

docs.title: AI query rewrites
docs.text:
Submit any query ID to get an LLM-generated optimization report. The report includes:

  • Rewrite — optimized SQL with inline comments explaining each change
  • Root Cause — why the original query is expensive (1–2 sentences)
  • Recommendations — clustering keys, filter pushdowns, warehouse right-sizing (bullet list)
  • Estimated Savings — rough credit reduction as a percentage range

Rewrite results are persisted and returned idempotently — calling the endpoint again for the same query ID returns the cached result without a second LLM call.

LLM required

AI rewrites require a configured LLM provider (llm_provider + llm_api_key in your config). Run frostwatch demo to see pre-baked example rewrites without an API key.

API endpoints:

POST /api/insights/rewrites          { "query_id": "01b2c3d4-..." }
GET  /api/insights/rewrites/{id}     Fetch a previously generated rewrite

docs.title: Partition pruning analysis
docs.text:
Snowflake stores data in micro-partitions. When a query has good clustering key alignment, Snowflake prunes (skips) partitions that cannot contain matching rows. A query that scans 95 % of partitions is performing a near-full-table-scan — usually fixable with a clustering key or a better WHERE filter.

FrostWatch computes the pruning ratio (partitions_scanned / partitions_total) for every query that has partition metadata, groups results by SQL fingerprint, and surfaces patterns where the average ratio is high and the credit cost is significant.

Avg pruning ratio Severity 50 % – 69 % medium 70 % – 89 % high ≥ 90 % critical

Each result includes a tailored recommendation (add a clustering key, push selective filters earlier, etc.) and the average/total credits consumed so you can prioritise fixes by ROI.

Small tables are excluded

Tables with fewer than 100 average partitions are excluded by default — full scans on small tables are cheap and not worth the noise. Adjust the min_partitions query parameter to raise or lower this threshold.

API endpoint: GET /api/insights/pruning?days=30&limit=20&min_partitions=100&min_ratio=0.5

docs.title: Demo mode
docs.text:
frostwatch demo pre-seeds two realistic rewrite examples — an ML features query and a MERGE statement — so the Insights page is immediately populated when you try the demo. No LLM API key required.

pip install frostwatch
frostwatch demo
# → open http://localhost:8000 → Insights

frostwatch config init   # creates ~/.frostwatch/config.yaml with defaults

Edit ~/.frostwatch/config.yaml and fill in your Snowflake credentials and LLM API key, then:

frostwatch serve         # API + UI on http://localhost:8000

On first start FrostWatch will not have any data — click Sync Now in the sidebar to pull the last 30 days of query history from Snowflake.

docs.title: Snowflake permissions
docs.text:
FrostWatch only needs read access to the ACCOUNT_USAGE schema. Create a dedicated role:

CREATE ROLE frostwatch;
GRANT IMPORTED PRIVILEGES ON DATABASE SNOWFLAKE TO ROLE frostwatch;
GRANT ROLE frostwatch TO USER my_service_user;

Then set snowflake_role: frostwatch in your config.

docs.title: FrostWatch launch kit (v0.5, Savings Advisor)

The hook for every post is the same: "Run one command, see how much your Snowflake account is wasting, with the SQL to fix it." Lead with the audit, not the dashboard. People try a 60-second command; they do not try a self-hosted server from a cold post.

Always link the sample report so people can see the output without installing anything: https://arunrajiah.github.io/frostwatch/sample-audit.html

docs.text:
Title: I built a free CLI that audits your Snowflake account for wasted spend in about a minute (open source, read-only)

Body:

After cleaning up the same handful of Snowflake cost problems at a few teams (auto-suspend left at 10 minutes, a Medium warehouse running 2 second queries, dashboards missing the result cache, Time Travel bigger than the table itself), I turned the checks into a tool.

pip install frostwatch && frostwatch audit -c <your connection>

It reads ACCOUNT_USAGE (read-only), runs 11 checks, and writes an HTML report with a dollar estimate and the exact SQL fix for each finding. Works with SSO, key-pair and connections.toml. No server, no LLM key, nothing leaves your machine.

Sample report: https://arunrajiah.github.io/frostwatch/sample-audit.html No Python? There is a single SQL script you can paste into Snowsight: https://github.com/arunrajiah/frostwatch/blob/main/sql/frostwatch_quick_audit.sql

It is MIT licensed. If you want continuous monitoring there is also a self-hosted dashboard (anomalies, cost per dbt model, query regressions, weekly Slack digest), but the audit stands on its own.

I would love feedback on the estimates: which checks are wrong for your setup, and what checks you would add.

Rules: r/dataengineering allows self-promo if you engage in comments. Reply to every comment for the first 3 hours.

docs.title: Quick Audit SQL (zero install)
docs.text:
Paste this into a Snowsight worksheet and click Run All. The final result lists findings sorted by estimated monthly savings, each with the SQL to fix it. Read-only.

It covers six core checks (auto-suspend, never-suspending warehouses, oversized warehouses, remote spilling, cloud services overage, missing resource monitors). The frostwatch audit CLI adds repeated-query, Time Travel bloat, unused-table and clustering checks, plus a shareable report.

Download the .sql file

-- =============================================================================
-- FrostWatch Quick Audit: find Snowflake savings in 60 seconds, zero install.
--
-- How to use: paste this whole file into a Snowsight worksheet and click
-- "Run All" (Cmd/Ctrl + Shift + Enter). The last result is your findings list,
-- sorted by estimated monthly savings, with the SQL to fix each one.
--
-- Read-only. Needs a role that can read SNOWFLAKE.ACCOUNT_USAGE
-- (ACCOUNTADMIN, or: GRANT DATABASE ROLE SNOWFLAKE.USAGE_VIEWER TO ROLE <role>).
--
-- Want more checks (repeated queries, Time Travel bloat, unused tables,
-- clustering costs), a shareable HTML report, and continuous monitoring?
--   pip install frostwatch && frostwatch audit
--   https://github.com/arunrajiah/frostwatch   (free, MIT, self-hosted)
-- =============================================================================

SET credit_price = 3.00;   -- USD per credit: change to your contract rate
SET days = 30;             -- history window

SHOW WAREHOUSES;
SET wh_qid = LAST_QUERY_ID();

WITH
wh AS (
    SELECT "name" AS name, "size" AS size, "auto_suspend" AS auto_suspend,
           "resource_monitor" AS resource_monitor,
           DECODE(UPPER(REPLACE("size", '-', '')),
                  'XSMALL', 1, 'SMALL', 2, 'MEDIUM', 4, 'LARGE', 8, 'XLARGE', 16,
                  '2XLARGE', 32, 'XXLARGE', 32, '3XLARGE', 64, 'XXXLARGE', 64,
                  '4XLARGE', 128, '5XLARGE', 256, '6XLARGE', 512, 0) AS cph
    FROM TABLE(RESULT_SCAN($wh_qid))
),
metering AS (
    SELECT warehouse_name, SUM(credits_used) AS credits,
           COUNT(DISTINCT DATE_TRUNC('hour', start_time)) AS active_hours
    FROM SNOWFLAKE.ACCOUNT_USAGE.WAREHOUSE_METERING_HISTORY
    WHERE start_time >= DATEADD('day', -$days, CURRENT_TIMESTAMP())
    GROUP BY 1
),
resumes AS (
    SELECT warehouse_name, COUNT(*) AS resumes
    FROM SNOWFLAKE.ACCOUNT_USAGE.WAREHOUSE_EVENTS_HISTORY
    WHERE timestamp >= DATEADD('day', -$days, CURRENT_TIMESTAMP())
      AND event_name = 'RESUME_WAREHOUSE' AND event_state = 'COMPLETED'
    GROUP BY 1
),
qstats AS (
    SELECT warehouse_name, COUNT(*) AS queries,
           APPROX_PERCENTILE(execution_time, 0.95) / 1000 AS p95_exec_s,
           APPROX_PERCENTILE(bytes_scanned, 0.95) AS p95_bytes,
           SUM(bytes_spilled_to_remote_storage) AS spill_remote,
           SUM(bytes_spilled_to_local_storage) AS spill_local
    FROM SNOWFLAKE.ACCOUNT_USAGE.QUERY_HISTORY
    WHERE start_time >= DATEADD('day', -$days, CURRENT_TIMESTAMP())
      AND warehouse_name IS NOT NULL AND execution_status = 'SUCCESS'
    GROUP BY 1
),
cs AS (
    SELECT SUM(credits_used_cloud_services) AS cs_credits,
           SUM(credits_used_cloud_services + credits_adjustment_cloud_services) AS cs_billed,
           SUM(credits_used_compute) AS compute_credits
    FROM SNOWFLAKE.ACCOUNT_USAGE.METERING_DAILY_HISTORY
    WHERE usage_date >= DATEADD('day', -$days, CURRENT_DATE())
),
findings AS (
    -- 1. Auto-suspend higher than 60s: idle tail after every resume is billed
    SELECT 'Auto-suspend set too high' AS finding, wh.name AS object_name,
           (wh.auto_suspend - 60) * COALESCE(r.resumes, m.active_hours / 2) / 3600
             * wh.cph * $credit_price * 30 / $days AS est_monthly_savings_usd,
           'AUTO_SUSPEND = ' || wh.auto_suspend || 's, ' || COALESCE(r.resumes, 0)
             || ' resumes in ' || $days || ' days' AS detail,
           'ALTER WAREHOUSE "' || wh.name || '" SET AUTO_SUSPEND = 60;' AS fix_sql
    FROM wh JOIN metering m ON m.warehouse_name = wh.name
    LEFT JOIN resumes r ON r.warehouse_name = wh.name
    WHERE wh.auto_suspend > 60

    UNION ALL
    -- 2. Auto-suspend disabled on a warehouse that bills around the clock
    SELECT 'Warehouse never suspends', wh.name,
           m.credits * $credit_price * 30 / $days * 0.5,
           'AUTO_SUSPEND is off; billed in ' || m.active_hours || ' of '
             || ($days * 24) || ' hours (savings assume half is idle)',
           'ALTER WAREHOUSE "' || wh.name || '" SET AUTO_SUSPEND = 60;'
    FROM wh JOIN metering m ON m.warehouse_name = wh.name
    WHERE COALESCE(wh.auto_suspend, 0) = 0 AND m.active_hours >= 0.8 * $days * 24

    UNION ALL
    -- 3. Oversized: Medium+ running only small, fast queries with no spilling
    SELECT 'Warehouse looks oversized', wh.name,
           m.credits * $credit_price * 30 / $days * 0.3,
           wh.size || ': ' || q.queries || ' queries, p95 ' || ROUND(q.p95_exec_s, 1)
             || 's, p95 scan ' || ROUND(q.p95_bytes / POWER(1024, 2)) || ' MB, no spilling',
           'ALTER WAREHOUSE "' || wh.name || '" SET WAREHOUSE_SIZE = '''
             || DECODE(wh.cph, 4, 'SMALL', 8, 'MEDIUM', 16, 'LARGE', 32, 'XLARGE',
                       64, 'XXLARGE', 128, 'XXXLARGE', 256, 'X4LARGE', 512, 'X5LARGE')
             || ''';  -- try for a week, compare runtimes'
    FROM wh JOIN metering m ON m.warehouse_name = wh.name
    JOIN qstats q ON q.warehouse_name = wh.name
    WHERE wh.cph >= 4 AND q.queries >= 100 AND q.p95_exec_s < 10
      AND q.p95_bytes < POWER(1024, 3) AND q.spill_remote = 0
      AND q.spill_local < POWER(1024, 3)

    UNION ALL
    -- 4. Remote spilling: undersized for some queries (performance risk)
    SELECT 'Queries spilling to remote storage', q.warehouse_name, 0,
           ROUND(q.spill_remote / POWER(1024, 3)) || ' GB spilled to remote storage',
           'SELECT query_id, bytes_spilled_to_remote_storage FROM SNOWFLAKE.ACCOUNT_USAGE.QUERY_HISTORY WHERE warehouse_name = '''
             || q.warehouse_name || ''' ORDER BY 2 DESC LIMIT 20;'
    FROM qstats q
    WHERE q.spill_remote > 10 * POWER(1024, 3)

    UNION ALL
    -- 5. Cloud services billed above the free 10 percent
    SELECT 'Paying for cloud services above the free 10 percent', 'ACCOUNT',
           cs.cs_billed * $credit_price * 30 / $days * 0.5,
           ROUND(cs.cs_billed, 1) || ' cloud services credits billed ('
             || ROUND(100 * cs.cs_credits / NULLIF(cs.compute_credits, 0)) || ' pct of compute)',
           'SELECT query_type, COUNT(*), SUM(credits_used_cloud_services) FROM SNOWFLAKE.ACCOUNT_USAGE.QUERY_HISTORY GROUP BY 1 ORDER BY 3 DESC LIMIT 20;'
    FROM cs
    WHERE cs.cs_billed > 0

    UNION ALL
    -- 6. No resource monitor: no ceiling on a runaway query
    SELECT 'Warehouse with no spending cap', wh.name, 0,
           'Spends ~$' || ROUND(m.credits * $credit_price * 30 / $days) || '/month with no resource monitor',
           'CREATE RESOURCE MONITOR "FW_' || wh.name || '_MONTHLY" WITH CREDIT_QUOTA = '
             || GREATEST(10, CEIL(m.credits * 30 / $days * 1.5))
             || ' FREQUENCY = MONTHLY START_TIMESTAMP = IMMEDIATELY TRIGGERS ON 80 PERCENT DO NOTIFY ON 100 PERCENT DO SUSPEND; ALTER WAREHOUSE "'
             || wh.name || '" SET RESOURCE_MONITOR = "FW_' || wh.name || '_MONTHLY";'
    FROM wh JOIN metering m ON m.warehouse_name = wh.name
    WHERE wh.resource_monitor IS NULL OR wh.resource_monitor = 'null'
)
SELECT ROW_NUMBER() OVER (ORDER BY est_monthly_savings_usd DESC, finding) AS rank,
       finding,
       object_name,
       ROUND(est_monthly_savings_usd, 2) AS est_monthly_savings_usd,
       detail,
       fix_sql
FROM findings
WHERE est_monthly_savings_usd >= 5 OR est_monthly_savings_usd = 0
ORDER BY rank;

docs.title: Resource Monitor Management
docs.text: FrostWatch v0.4 adds end-to-end resource monitor management: it reads your existing Snowflake monitors, analyses warehouse spend patterns, recommends optimal quotas, generates copy-paste DDL, and alerts you when a monitor is approaching its limit.

docs.title: What are resource monitors?
docs.text:
A Snowflake resource monitor is a named object that enforces a credit quota on one or more virtual warehouses. When a warehouse reaches the configured percentage of its quota, Snowflake can:

  • Notify — send an email to account admins
  • Suspend — gracefully stop new queries when running queries finish
  • Suspend immediately — kill all running queries and suspend the warehouse

Resource monitors are the primary mechanism for preventing runaway costs in Snowflake. FrostWatch automates the tedious parts: analysing historical spend, choosing the right quota, and writing the SQL.

docs.title: Viewing existing monitors
docs.text:
After a sync, navigate to Resource Monitors in the sidebar to see all monitors cached from SNOWFLAKE.ACCOUNT_USAGE.RESOURCE_MONITORS. For each monitor you'll see:

  • Current quota, used credits, and remaining credits
  • Assigned warehouses
  • Trigger thresholds (notify / suspend / suspend-immediately)
  • Reset frequency (MONTHLY, DAILY, WEEKLY, YEARLY)

Tip

If you have no resource monitors yet, this list will be empty — but the Recommendations tab will still work from your warehouse metering history.

docs.title: Recommendations
docs.text:
The Recommendations tab analyses the last 30 days of warehouse metering history (configurable) and suggests a monthly credit quota for each warehouse:

monthly_quota = p95_daily_credits × 30 × (1 + buffer_pct)

The quota is then rounded up to the nearest clean milestone (10, 25, 50, 100, 250, 500, 1 000, 2 500, 5 000, 10 000 credits) so your CREATE RESOURCE MONITOR statements use human-readable numbers.

Each recommendation includes:

Field Description avg_daily_credits Simple mean over the history window p95_daily_credits 95th-percentile daily usage — resists outlier days recommended_quota Rounded monthly quota recommended_cost_usd Estimated monthly cost at your credits_per_dollar rate quota_status uncovered, undersized, oversized, or adequate priority high, medium, or low (based on spend level and volatility)

quota_status thresholds:

Status Condition uncovered No existing monitor for this warehouse undersized Current quota is less than 77 % of recommended oversized Current quota is more than 143 % of recommended adequate Current quota is within ±30 % of recommended

docs.title: Tuning the analysis
docs.text:
You can adjust two query parameters:

  • history_days (7–90, default 30) — use fewer days for faster-changing workloads
  • buffer_pct (0–1.0, default 0.20) — increase the buffer if you have highly variable workloads

docs.title: Generating DDL
docs.text:
Click Generate SQL next to any recommendation (or call GET /api/resource-monitors/generate-sql?warehouse=MY_WH) to get a complete CREATE OR REPLACE RESOURCE MONITOR statement:

-- Resource monitor for TRANSFORM_WH
-- Based on 30 days of history
-- Avg daily credits: 0.85  |  P95 daily: 1.42  |  Est. monthly cost: $16.67
CREATE OR REPLACE RESOURCE MONITOR RM_TRANSFORM_WH
    WITH CREDIT_QUOTA = 50            -- MONTHLY credit limit
    FREQUENCY = MONTHLY
    START_TIMESTAMP = IMMEDIATELY
    TRIGGERS
        ON 75  PERCENT DO NOTIFY    -- email account admins
        ON 100  PERCENT DO SUSPEND  -- suspend all warehouses on this monitor
        ON 110 PERCENT DO SUSPEND_IMMEDIATE;

-- Assign the monitor to the warehouse
ALTER WAREHOUSE TRANSFORM_WH SET RESOURCE_MONITOR = RM_TRANSFORM_WH;

Copy the statement into a Snowflake worksheet and run it as a user with the CREATE RESOURCE MONITOR privilege (typically ACCOUNTADMIN or SYSADMIN).

docs.title: Proximity alerts
docs.text:
The Proximity Alerts tab shows which monitors are approaching their credit limits so you can act before workloads are unexpectedly suspended.

Severity Condition 🔴 Critical Within 5 percentage points of a trigger threshold 🟠 High Within 15 percentage points of a trigger threshold 🟡 Medium Trigger is ahead but more than 15 pp away

Alerts are computed from the last synced used_credits / credit_quota ratio — run a fresh sync to get up-to-date values.

docs.title: Per-user and per-role budgets
docs.text:
FrostWatch can track credit spend against configurable daily limits for individual users and roles. Configure them in config.yaml:

user_credit_budgets:
  ANALYST_ALICE: 5.0    # daily credit limit
  DBT_SVC: 50.0
  ML_TEAM_SVC: 20.0

role_credit_budgets:
  ANALYST: 15.0
  TRANSFORMER: 10.0

The Budgets tab (or GET /api/resource-monitors/budgets?days=7) shows:

  • Credits consumed in the selected window
  • Daily budget and period budget (daily × days)
  • Percentage of budget used
  • Whether the entity is over-budget for the period

Note

Budget tracking uses the CachedQuery data already fetched during sync — it does not require any additional Snowflake permissions beyond what FrostWatch already uses.

docs.title: Required Snowflake permissions
docs.text:
To sync existing resource monitors FrostWatch needs:

GRANT IMPORTED PRIVILEGES ON DATABASE SNOWFLAKE TO ROLE <frostwatch_role>;

This permission is already needed for query history and warehouse metering. No additional permissions are required for reading RESOURCE_MONITORS.

To apply the generated DDL in Snowflake:

GRANT CREATE RESOURCE MONITOR ON ACCOUNT TO ROLE SYSADMIN;

FrostWatch never applies DDL automatically — it only generates SQL for you to review and run.

docs.title: Savings Advisor and frostwatch audit
docs.text:
Find out how much your Snowflake account is overspending in about a minute. No server, no config file, no LLM key. Read-only.

pip install frostwatch          # or: uvx frostwatch audit ...
frostwatch audit --connection my_snowflake

You get a ranked list of findings in the terminal and a shareable HTML report (frostwatch-audit.html) with a dollar estimate and copy-paste fix SQL for each one. See a sample report

docs.title: Connecting
docs.text:
Pick whichever matches how you already log in:

You use Command Snowflake CLI / connections.toml frostwatch audit -c <connection_name> SSO (Okta, Azure AD, ...) frostwatch audit -a <account> -u <user> (opens your browser) Key-pair service user frostwatch audit -a <account> -u <user> --private-key rsa_key.p8 Password (no MFA) SNOWFLAKE_PASSWORD=... frostwatch audit -a <account> -u <user> --authenticator snowflake Just looking frostwatch audit --demo

Add --role if your default role cannot read SNOWFLAKE.ACCOUNT_USAGE. The minimum grant is:

GRANT DATABASE ROLE SNOWFLAKE.USAGE_VIEWER TO ROLE <your_role>;

docs.title: What it checks
docs.text:
Check Category How savings are estimated Auto-suspend higher than 60s Compute (auto_suspend minus 60s) x resumes x credits/hour Warehouse never suspends Compute 50 percent of the warehouse's spend Oversized warehouse (Medium+, p95 under 10s, under 1 GB scanned, no spill) Compute 30 percent of the warehouse's spend Identical query re-run without hitting the result cache Compute 50 percent of its runtime cost Cloud services billed above the free 10 percent Cloud services 50 percent of the billed amount Time Travel and Fail-safe larger than the table Storage Fail-safe plus 80 percent of Time Travel bytes x $/TB Large table not read in 90 days (Enterprise) Storage Its active bytes x $/TB Remote spilling Performance Flagged, no dollar estimate Queuing (concurrency bound) Performance Flagged, no dollar estimate Warehouse with no resource monitor Guardrails Flagged, with ready-made CREATE RESOURCE MONITOR SQL Expensive automatic clustering Compute Cost shown for review

Compute savings for one warehouse are capped at 70 percent of its spend so overlapping findings never double count. All estimates are directional: they are meant to rank where to look first, not to be quoted to finance to the cent.

docs.title: Options
docs.text:
--days 30              History window (7 to 365)
--output report.md     .html (default), .md (paste into Slack or a GitHub issue), or .json
--price 2.40           Your contract price per credit (default 3.00)
--storage-price 23     USD per TB-month
--fail-over 500        Exit with code 2 if monthly savings exceed $500 (use in CI)
--no-open              Do not open the report in a browser

docs.title: In the web UI
docs.text: When you run frostwatch serve, an audit runs after every scheduled sync and shows on the Savings page, with a Run audit now button and a link to the shareable report. API: GET /api/advisor, POST /api/advisor/run, GET /api/advisor/report.html, GET /api/advisor/report.md.

docs.title: Weekly audit in GitHub Actions
docs.text:
name: Snowflake savings audit
on:
  schedule: [{ cron: "0 8 * * 1" }]
  workflow_dispatch:
jobs:
  audit:
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    steps:
      - run: echo "${{ secrets.SNOWFLAKE_PRIVATE_KEY }}" > key.p8
      - run: >
          pipx run frostwatch audit --no-open -o audit.md
          -a ${{ vars.SNOWFLAKE_ACCOUNT }} -u ${{ vars.SNOWFLAKE_USER }}
          --private-key key.p8 --role FROSTWATCH_ROLE
      - run: cat audit.md >> "$GITHUB_STEP_SUMMARY"

docs.title: No install at all
docs.text: Can't install Python where you are? Paste the Quick Audit SQL into a Snowsight worksheet instead.

docs.title: Snowflake cost optimization checklist
docs.text:
Most Snowflake bills carry 15 to 40 percent of avoidable spend, and it hides in the same handful of places. Here is the checklist we use, ordered by how often it pays off, with the query to find each issue and the fix. Every item is automated by frostwatch audit and the Quick Audit SQL.

Skip the reading

pip install frostwatch && frostwatch audit -c <connection> runs all of these in about a minute and writes a report with dollar estimates. Sample report.

docs.title: 1. Set auto-suspend to 60 seconds
docs.text:
Snowflake bills a minimum of 60 seconds per resume, then per second. A warehouse with AUTO_SUSPEND = 600 burns up to nine idle minutes after every burst of work. On a Large warehouse (8 credits/hour) that resumes 10 times a day, that is about 12 credits a day for nothing.

SHOW WAREHOUSES;  -- check the auto_suspend column
ALTER WAREHOUSE my_wh SET AUTO_SUSPEND = 60;

Exception: BI warehouses that benefit from a warm local disk cache can justify 5 to 10 minutes. Measure before and after.

docs.title: 2. Never leave auto-suspend off
docs.text: AUTO_SUSPEND = 0 or NULL means the warehouse runs until someone stops it. It is the single most expensive one-line mistake in Snowflake.

docs.title: 3. Right-size warehouses that only run small queries
docs.text: Each size up doubles the credit rate. If a Medium or larger warehouse only runs queries that finish in a few seconds and scan little data, one size down usually costs half with barely any slowdown. Look at p95 runtime and bytes scanned per warehouse in QUERY_HISTORY, and make sure nothing spills.

docs.title: 4. Upsize (or fix) only what spills to remote storage
docs.text: BYTES_SPILLED_TO_REMOTE_STORAGE > 0 means the query ran out of memory and local disk. These queries can run many times slower. Fix the query, or route only those jobs to a bigger warehouse: upsizing everything to fix a few queries is a classic overspend.

docs.title: 5. Treat queuing with clusters, not size
docs.text: If queries spend a lot of time in QUEUED_OVERLOAD_TIME, you have a concurrency problem. A multi-cluster warehouse (Enterprise) with SCALING_POLICY = 'ECONOMY' adds capacity only while the queue exists. A bigger single cluster costs more all day.

docs.title: 6. Make the result cache work for dashboards
docs.text: Identical queries normally hit the 24-hour result cache for free. They miss it when the SQL uses CURRENT_TIMESTAMP(), RANDOM() or similar, when USE_CACHED_RESULT = FALSE, or when the table changes between runs. Group QUERY_HISTORY by QUERY_HASH, look for hashes that ran hundreds of times and still scanned data, and fix the SQL or materialize the result.

docs.title: 7. Stay under the free 10 percent of cloud services
docs.text: Cloud services credits are free up to 10 percent of daily compute. Above that you pay. Check METERING_DAILY_HISTORY: credits_used_cloud_services + credits_adjustment_cloud_services is the billed part. Usual causes: very chatty tools issuing thousands of tiny queries or SHOW commands, and huge compilation workloads.

docs.title: 8. Cut Time Travel and Fail-safe on churny tables
docs.text: Tables rebuilt from scratch or heavily updated keep every old version for the retention period, plus 7 days of Fail-safe. In TABLE_STORAGE_METRICS, look for tables where time_travel_bytes + failsafe_bytes exceeds active_bytes. If the table can be rebuilt from source, make it transient and set DATA_RETENTION_TIME_IN_DAYS = 0 or 1. In dbt, +transient: true.

docs.title: 9. Find large tables nobody reads
docs.text: On Enterprise Edition, ACCESS_HISTORY tells you which tables were read. Big tables with no reads in 90 days are candidates to drop or unload to object storage. Confirm with owners first.

docs.title: 10. Put a resource monitor on every warehouse
docs.text:
Resource monitors are free and are the only hard stop for a runaway query or a loop gone wrong. A monthly quota at about 1.5x normal usage, notify at 80 percent and suspend at 100 percent, costs nothing in normal months.

CREATE RESOURCE MONITOR wh_monthly WITH CREDIT_QUOTA = 500 FREQUENCY = MONTHLY
  START_TIMESTAMP = IMMEDIATELY
  TRIGGERS ON 80 PERCENT DO NOTIFY ON 100 PERCENT DO SUSPEND;
ALTER WAREHOUSE my_wh SET RESOURCE_MONITOR = wh_monthly;

FrostWatch's resource monitor page sizes quotas from your real p95 spend.

docs.title: 11. Review automatic clustering spend
docs.text: Automatic clustering runs serverless and can quietly cost more than the queries it speeds up. Check AUTOMATIC_CLUSTERING_HISTORY per table, and confirm queries actually filter on the clustering key.

docs.title: Keep it from creeping back
docs.text: A one-off cleanup decays in weeks: a new dbt model, a new dashboard, a new hire with a Large warehouse. FrostWatch watches continuously: anomaly alerts, cost per dbt model, week-over-week query regressions, AI query rewrites and a weekly Slack digest. Free, MIT licensed, self-hosted.
